desc: Skunk Works is the physical and cultural template for how an unacknowledged program is run inside a private corporation. Founded by Clarence 'Kelly' Johnson in 1943 and led by Ben Rich from 1975 to 1991, it produced the U-2, the A-12/SR-71, the F-117, Sea Shadow, DarkStar and the RQ-170 Sentinel - the last of which existed operationally for years before Lockheed acknowledged it, which is the point. AARO's Historical Record Report itself uses Skunk Works aircraft as the explanation for a class of UAP reports, conceding in the process that the organisation routinely fields flying hardware whose existence the government denies while it is flying. Its home is Air Force Plant 42 at Palmdale, a government-owned contractor-operated facility whose accreditation architecture supports program-level compartmentation. For this domain Skunk Works matters in two ways. It is the operational proof that a prime contractor can hold, fly and conceal an object of unknown provenance from everyone without a need to know, including senior officers in the chain of command. And it is the organisation Ben Rich ran, whose post-retirement remarks about technologies 'locked up in black projects' are the most quoted and least documented artifact in the entire field.

dossier.denialPosture: Skunk Works does not deny; it declines to confirm, and the record shows the decline holding for years at a time and then ending on someone else's timetable. The RQ-170 is the canonical instance: operational, photographed, and unacknowledged until it was lost abroad. The 1986 GAO exchange is the same posture at the paperwork layer -- GAO was granted access on condition that it not name the programme, the component or the service, so the public record of the failure exists with the subject of the failure redacted out of it. The board treats that as a documented behaviour rather than an inference, because in both cases the concealment and its terms are described in a government document.
dossier.narrative:
The reason Skunk Works belongs at programme level on this board is not that anyone has documented anomalous material inside it. It is that Skunk Works settles an argument the board otherwise has to make by inference. The standing objection to every legacy-programme account is that a secret of this size could not be kept -- too many people, too many decades, too many contractors. Skunk Works is the counter-example the United States government publishes about itself: the RQ-170 flew operationally for years before Lockheed acknowledged it existed, and the acknowledgment came after a loss on foreign soil rather than on a schedule anyone chose. The concealment worked until physics interrupted it.

What the 1986 GAO material adds is the failure mode. Concealment of that quality is not free, and the price is paid in accountability: 1,460 discrepancies in a 40,000-item special-access inventory at one company, 11 still unresolved, discovered because a congressional subcommittee asked rather than because the security system surfaced it. GAO's own explanation of why nobody caught it earlier is the sentence this board keeps returning to -- special access contracts are 'carved out of the Defense Investigative Service's periodic inspection program', by a 1965 decision, and by 1983 there were probably several thousand of them.

The organisation therefore sits on this board twice over: as the demonstration that unacknowledged hardware can be held indefinitely, and as the documented case where holding it meant nobody could say where the paper went.
openQuestions: GAO/NSIAD-88-2BR, 'Information Security: Actions Taken To Improve Lockheed's Special Access Document Accountability', is the follow-up that would say whether anything changed after 1986. It appeared in a search result only and has not been opened; nothing on this board is cited to it.

The 1986 testimony and its companion report never name the special access programme itself, by agreement with DoD. Whether that programme has since been acknowledged, and under what name, is not established from any document read here.

Ben Rich's post-retirement remarks about technologies 'locked up in black projects' remain the most quoted and least documented artefact in this field. No primary recording or contemporaneous transcript has been located, and the board carries no Tier 1 or Tier 2 claim resting on them.
dossier.whatItIs: Lockheed Martin Advanced Development Programs, universally known as Skunk Works: the unacknowledged-program aeronautics organisation founded by Clarence 'Kelly' Johnson in 1943 at Burbank, California, and now resident at Air Force Plant 42, Palmdale, a government-owned contractor-operated facility. Ben Rich directed it from 1975 to 1991. Its programme list is the working definition of the black aircraft: the U-2, the A-12 and SR-71, the F-117, Sea Shadow, DarkStar and the RQ-170 Sentinel.
dossier.whyImplicated: Skunk Works is the operational proof of the board's central structural claim: that a private corporation can hold, fly and conceal hardware from everyone without a need to know, including senior officers in the chain of command, for years at a time. AARO's own Historical Record Report uses Skunk Works aircraft to explain a class of UAP reports, and in doing so concedes the point -- the organisation routinely fields flying objects whose existence the government denies while they are flying. As of the 1986 GAO pass it also carries a documented custody failure: the companion report to GAO's testimony of 24 July 1986 names the Lockheed/Burbank plant as the site where special-access document control deteriorated, and says the deterioration might not have happened had the Defense Investigative Service been permitted to inspect the contract as it inspected Lockheed's others.
